The clearest dimension on which the methods differ is the component changed in the metric pipeline. K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN primarily alter representation learning: K-tuplet compares an anchor jointly with K negatives and uses semi-hard mining, whereas Proto-Triplet/ICNN explicitly encode intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. Prototypical or nearest-mean methods alter class aggregation by representing each class with a mean vector and applying a fixed geometric decision. Relation networks alter the decision rule by learning a nonlinear comparator from paired query and support features. RCN also learns a comparator, but its experimental contribution includes local region correspondence and Region Activation Mapping interpretability, not only accuracy. SRL and DSN alter class geometry by replacing or supplementing point vectors with subspaces; SRL uses weighted subspace distance plus prototypical or discriminative template subspaces, while DSN uses SVD-constructed class subspaces and projection distance. Cross-domain experiments separate embedding robustness from in-domain episodic fit more directly. Deep K-tuplet Network was trained on miniImageNet and then evaluated on novel classes in Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars; the authors report that it significantly outperforms prior methods in that cross-dataset setting and interpret the result as evidence that the learned discriminative embedding generalizes beyond the training dataset. The Proto-Triplet/ICNN study similarly reports competitive generalization to CUB, Dogs and Cars. MSENet reports cross-domain testing across eight benchmark datasets after evaluating 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot tasks on MiniImageNet and FC100. These results support the embedding-side hypothesis that transferable feature geometry helps under domain shift, but the studies do not provide enough matched information in the cited excerpts to compare their exact cross-domain accuracies with each other or to attribute gains solely to the loss when architecture and training details differ. Subspace methods are supported by a different experimental argument: richer class descriptions can reduce sensitivity to noisy or outlying support examples. The deep metric-learning review states that Deep Subspace Network, which builds low-dimensional class subspaces from support samples and assigns a query by distance to its projection, is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network. SRL evaluates its image-level subspace representation and K-shot prototypical or discriminative template subspaces on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and CUB and reports competitive or superior performance compared with previous state-of-the-art methods in its experiments. These findings are directly relevant when local spatial structure and within-image or within-class diversity are lost by global vector pooling, but they do not establish superiority in one-shot settings where estimating a subspace from support variation may be poorly constrained. RCN's experiments should be interpreted along both accuracy and explainability axes. The method compares related local regions between query and support images and uses Region Activation Mapping to visualize intermediate comparison variables. Its paper reports extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets and effectiveness over existing baselines, while also generalizing explanations from tasks to categories and identifying prototypical parts. This makes RCN comparatively strong on the sourced criterion of interpretable local matching. It is not experimentally interchangeable with SRL: RCN exposes region-to-region evidence for a match, whereas SRL preserves spatial structure through subspace representations and weighted subspace distance. Without a common table using the same encoder, episodes and baselines, the cited evidence supports complementarity rather than a numerical ranking between region explanations and subspace geometry. Fixed-metric and learned-metric methods also trade simplicity for flexibility. Cosine matching, Euclidean distance to class means, ridge regression and graph-based comparison are surveyed as metric-learning choices, while relation networks explicitly learn a nonlinear relation module instead of relying on a fixed metric. The empirical implication is that fixed rules are easier to deploy and remain feed-forward, but they can only separate classes well when the encoder and class representation already satisfy the metric geometry. Learned relation modules can model more complex match relations, but their reported gains depend on episodic training and may reflect comparator overfitting if the training task distribution differs from the test domain. The cited sources support this mechanism-level trade-off; they do not supply a universal accuracy advantage for learned over fixed distances across all benchmarks. The cross-family Meta-Dataset/VTAB study is an important warning against treating episodic metric results as isolated evidence of best few-shot performance. It compares leading transfer and meta-learning approaches under both Meta-Dataset and VTAB and finds that, on average, large-scale BiT transfer methods outperform competing approaches on Meta-Dataset even when trained only on ImageNet, whereas meta-learning approaches trained and validated on Meta-Dataset struggle to compete on VTAB. The same study reports that increasing scale does not improve performance on highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. Because BiT is a large-scale pretraining and fine-tuning comparator rather than a pure metric learner, this result does not show that transfer is a better metric; it shows that metric methods must be compared under matched data scale and adaptation protocol before claiming state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy. Specialized modalities further limit generalization of natural-image rankings. The FewSAR benchmark for few-shot SAR target classification implements 15 classic methods in three categories, establishes common protocols, and analyzes both quantitative results and runtime under the same setting. Its authors observe that metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy in that SAR testbed, while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, which they attribute primarily to bias in existing datasets. This is evidence for metric learning within the SAR benchmark and protocol, not evidence that the same ranking holds for MiniImageNet, CUB or Meta-Dataset. It also illustrates why runtime and dataset bias, when measured under a unified benchmark, are useful comparison dimensions that most natural-image method quotes do not provide. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:d132e7c0300c]

Taken together, the sourced experiments support conditional conclusions rather than a single winner. Embedding-loss methods are best supported for improving latent-space separation and cross-dataset transfer in their reported protocols; point prototypes and fixed metrics offer simple feed-forward baselines; relation and region networks add learned nonlinear or local matching, with RCN additionally providing visual explanations; distributional and subspace models target uncertainty, spatial structure and robustness to support noise; and multi-stage encoders target the use of shallow through abstract features. Direct numerical ranking is possible only inside a paper's matched table or a unified benchmark such as the SAR study or the controlled cross-family transfer/meta study. Across the other cited papers, unmatched datasets, backbones, training sources, shot counts, class-representation assumptions and fine-tuning regimes make isolated accuracy claims non-comparable, even when each paper individually reports competitive or superior performance. Limitations and Open Problems

A central estimation issue is that different metric-learning designs place different demands on scarce support information. A point prototype summarizes support embeddings as one vector, a distributional model estimates class distributions with a neural network, and subspace models construct class or image subspaces from local CNN features or support samples. The review explicitly identifies single point-based metric learning as sensitive to noise and presents distributional and subspace representations as alternatives; SRL similarly motivates subspaces by the need to preserve spatial structure and diversity. These sources support the trade-off between simple class summaries and richer class representations, but they do not establish that every richer model is better estimated from the same few examples. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:a7488a94c25a] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:da87ef976a14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:3331491a245d]

A second issue is the distinction between fixed and learned distance measures. The surveyed metric choices include cosine similarity, Euclidean distance to class means, ridge regression, graph neural networks, and CNN-based relation modules. Fixed rules rely on the embedding and class representation to make the predefined comparison valid, whereas relation networks learn a nonlinear relation module from paired query and support features. The relation-network paper argues that this learned deep metric is more expressive than a manually fixed metric or linear classifier, but the cited evidence does not show that learned comparators are universally preferable or that their gains persist across unmatched backbones, episodes, and domains. Domain shift is a concrete limitation in the cited few-shot literature. Standard same-dataset episodes draw base and novel classes from the same domain, whereas the K-tuplet work introduces cross-dataset evaluation because it regards that setting as potentially unrepresentative of real-world use. It trains on miniImageNet and tests on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. Another metric-learning paper explicitly states that existing metric-based approaches often do not generalize well to categories from different domains. Therefore, same-domain episodic results and cross-dataset results answer different generalization questions and should not be merged into one accuracy ranking. The assumption of one shared metric across tasks is identified as restrictive by the Meta-Metric-Learner paper. It states that metric-based approaches learn one task-invariant metric and require tasks to come from a similar domain for that metric to work across tasks, while optimization-based approaches can handle flexible class counts but impose homogeneous task-specific classifier structure. Its hybrid response combines a task-specific metric-based base learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model. This identifies a trade-off between a single feed-forward comparator and added meta-learning machinery for flexible class counts and cross-task metrics. Representation-learning losses target latent-space geometry rather than every part of the metric pipeline. K-tuplet learning extends triplet training so that an anchor is compared jointly with K negative samples and uses semi-hard mining; Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses explicitly use intra-class and inter-class distance or nearest-neighbor criteria. The cited papers report favorable miniImageNet results and, for K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN, cross-domain results on additional datasets. These sources support embedding regularization as a distinct contribution, but they do not show that such losses alone replace class aggregation, local correspondence, distributional uncertainty, or subspace modeling. Benchmark and modality dependence is illustrated directly by FewSAR. The paper motivates a unified few-shot SAR benchmark because researchers have used their own datasets and setups, impeding comparison. Embedding losses target discriminative latent geometry; prototypes aggregate support vectors; distributional and subspace methods model uncertainty, variation, noise robustness, or spatial structure; relation and region networks learn nonlinear or local matching; and BiT represents a large-scale transfer-learning comparator. The strongest numerical comparisons are therefore within a paper's own matched experiments, the unified FewSAR protocol, or the controlled Meta-Dataset/VTAB cross-family study. Across the other sources, datasets, training sources, shot counts, backbones, adaptation procedures, and reported baselines differ, so competitive or superior within-paper claims should remain method- and protocol-specific. Conclusion

For the research question, the central trade-off is where each method accepts complexity. Embedding-focused losses are appropriate when class separability is the main bottleneck, but they do not solve aggregation, uncertainty or local correspondence by themselves. Mean prototypes and fixed cosine or Euclidean rules are simple and feed-forward, yet depend strongly on embedding geometry. Distributional and subspace representations can model variation and support noise, but their richer estimates may be unreliable with one or highly correlated support example. Learned relation modules offer flexible nonlinear matching, while RCN uniquely supplies region-level explanations in the cited evidence. Numerical superiority should be accepted only within matched tables or unified protocols; cross-domain, Meta-Dataset/VTAB, and FewSAR results answer different questions and cannot be merged into a general leaderboard. claim_records.text: The proposed Metric-Agnostic Conditional network (MACO) achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The MACO architecture conditions class representations for each few-shot trial based on a target query image, and trains a network to perform comparisons between classes rather than relying on a static metric comparison.
The MACO architecture is not a true metric-learning approach, as its output is a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric.
The MACO network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target query image.
The MACO network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: Feature Stage, Relational Stage, Conditioning Stage, and Classifier.

The Feature Stage of MACO uses a convolutional architecture identical to Ravi & Larochelle (2017), composed of four convolutional blocks each with a 3×3 kernel, 32 filters, batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, followed by a linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image vector.

The Relational Stage of MACO uses a relational network to compare images within a class in a pairwise fashion, producing a single vector to represent the class, with parameters shared across all classes.

claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid meta-learning model combines a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model with a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

The Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot learning setting and the new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in both single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, and thus can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Existing metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

The Meta-Metric-Learner's meta learner operates across tasks using an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model parameterized by weight predictions from the optimization-based meta-learner.

Because metric-based models are essentially non-parametric and not sensitive to the number of classes, the proposed Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets.

claim_records.text: A single metric is insufficient to capture complex task variations in the diverse natural language few-shot learning setting.
The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

The proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few-shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets.
The proposed task-clustering framework for diverse few-shot learning includes a task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion as its initial step.
Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires conducting source-target transfer learning O(n^2) times, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
For a large number of diverse tasks where n can be larger than 1,000, evaluation of the full transfer performance matrix is unacceptable due to over 1M entries to evaluate.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm randomly samples task pairs to evaluate Sij and Sji scores to address the large number of entries in the transfer performance matrix.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm keeps only task pairs (i, j) with consistent Sij and Sji scores to address unreliable entries and asymmetry issues.

Previous few-shot learning works mainly considered image domains where tasks are sampled from a single large data collection such as Omniglot or ImageNet, making tasks related and from a single domain.
In enterprise AI cloud service scenarios, submitted text classification tasks are significantly diverse, so a common metric is insufficient to handle all these tasks.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples according to their distances to few seen samples in an embedding space learned by powerful deep neural networks.
Deep metric learning methods can avoid overfitting to few training images in few-shot image classification and have achieved state-of-the-art performance.

The review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification from 2018 to 2022 into three groups according to three stages of metric learning: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of the novel class are classified by computing their distances to novel support images with respect to the learned measure, followed by applying a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-support pair similarities and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-prototype similarity pairs in the UAFS framework.
Extensive experiments show the proposed UAFS method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
For a query sample and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node in a graph-based model to jointly infer similarity uncertainty for each pair.
The network in the UAFS framework is optimized with similarity-based classification losses that exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.

fact_fields.method: Uncertainty-aware optimization with similarity-based classification losses

claim_records.text: In few-shot image classification, the logit vector (classification probability) for a query sample is obtained by feeding similarities between the query sample and prototypes to a SoftMax function.
The reliability of estimated similarity is vital to classification performance in few-shot image classification.
Aleatoric uncertainty captures noise inherent in observations and identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample.
An observed similarity of a query-prototype pair suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

For each query-prototype pair in the proposed framework, the observed feature similarity is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of the distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-based few-shot classification algorithms often fail to generalize to unseen domains due to large discrepancy of feature distributions across domains.
Feature-wise transformation layers using affine transforms are used to augment image features and simulate various feature distributions under different domains during training.

fact_fields.method: Feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

Metric-based few-shot classification methods consist of a feature encoder and a metric function, where the encoder extracts image features and the metric function predicts the category of query images using features of labeled and unlabeled images.
The distributions of image features extracted from tasks in unseen domains are significantly different from those in seen domains.
During training, the metric function may overfit to feature distributions encoded only from seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

Integrating feature-wise transformation layers into the feature encoder allows simulating various distributions of image features during training, improving the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

fact_fields.method: Feature-wise transformation layer integration into feature encoder

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn algorithm is developed to optimize the proposed feature-wise transformation layers so that the model works well on unseen domains after training using seen domains.

fact_fields.method: Learning-to-learn optimization of feature-wise transformation layers

claim_records.text: The proposed feature-wise transformation layers are method-agnostic and can be applied to various metric-based few-shot classification approaches for improving generalization to unseen domains.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for few-shot image classification that aims to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific related regions in query and support set images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCN is effective over existing baselines for few-shot image classification.
RCN's model indicates the relationship between final classification decision and region similarities directly in the last layer, which can be viewed as a simple and easily explained linear process.
The region meta learner in RCN is a dynamic system that aims to adapt to different meta tasks in the training and testing stage.
Few-shot learning methods are grouped into metric-based models and gradient-based models in this work.
Metric-based few-shot classification methods achieve classification score by computing similarity between support sample and query sample using metric methods such as Euclidean distance.
Gradient-based few-shot learning methods such as MAML and MetaSGD are usually model agnostic and can be used with metric learning models to achieve higher performance on few-shot learning tasks.

claim_records.text: Few-shot learning approaches can be grouped into two main categories: transfer learning and meta-learning.

Transfer learning approaches are best exemplified when less downstream data is available, and may in principle be applied to few-shot classification even though typical downstream tasks have thousands or more training examples.
VTAB+MD is a few-shot classification evaluation protocol introduced to facilitate exchanging and comparing ideas between the transfer learning and few-shot classification communities.

A carefully engineered training and fine-tuning of large scale networks exemplified by BiT is a remarkably competitive and robust baseline for few-shot classification, and generalizes across large-scale, multi-dataset benchmarks.
On average, large-scale transfer methods (Big Transfer, BiT) outperform competing approaches on the Meta-Dataset (MD) benchmark, even when trained only on ImageNet.
Meta-learning approaches struggle to compete on the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset (MD).
Pushing for scale does not improve BiT performance on highly out-of-distribution MD tasks.
Large vision models transfer well to popular classification benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR, etc.) and VTAB-1k.
Well-tuned transfer learning baselines are competitive with more complex few-shot classification approaches.

claim_records.text: The Relation Network (RN) is trained end-to-end from scratch, and during meta-learning it learns a deep distance metric to compare images within episodes designed to simulate the few-shot setting.
Once trained, a RN classifies images of new classes by computing relation scores between query images and the few examples of each new class without further updating the network.
The RN framework is easily extended to zero-shot learning, and extensive experiments on five benchmarks show it provides a unified and effective approach for both few-shot and zero-shot learning.

All few-shot learning experiments use Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 10^-3, annealed by half for every 100,000 episodes, and all models are end-to-end trained from scratch with no additional dataset.
The Omniglot dataset contains 1623 character classes from 50 different alphabets, each class contains 20 samples drawn by different people.

Following prior work, new classes are augmented through 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations of existing Omniglot data, with 1200 original classes plus rotations used for training and the remaining 423 classes plus rotations used for testing.
All input Omniglot images are resized to 28 × 28.

The RN approach learns a transferrable deep metric for comparing the relation between images (few-shot learning) or between images and class descriptions (zero-shot learning), rather than using a pre-defined fixed metric.

The RN training objective uses mean squared error (MSE) to minimize the difference between predicted relation scores and ground-truth targets, where matched pairs have similarity 1 and mismatched pairs have similarity 0.
Modifying the RN framework for zero-shot learning is straightforward: instead of a support set with one-shot image per class, a semantic class embedding vector is used for each class.

claim_records.text: Compared to prior metric-based few-shot approaches, RN provides a learnable rather than fixed metric, and a non-linear rather than linear classifier.

When applied to zero-shot learning, the RN architecture is related to methods that learn to align images and category embeddings and perform recognition by predicting if an image and category embedding pair match.
The RN benchmarks show it provides compelling performance across the board while being simpler and faster than alternative few-shot learning approaches.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features that are fully aligned with textual features representing the "Summary" of the image.
Local representations (LRs) at low-level are more consistent between seen and unseen samples compared to high-level representations.
The proposed Meta-Feature Adaption method (MF-Adapter) combines the complementary strengths of both low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.

Extensive experiments show the proposed MF-Adapter method is superior to state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, even showing stronger performance on a set of challenging visual classification tasks.
CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) learns high-quality visual representation by conducting contrastive learning with hundreds of millions of noisy text-image pairs.
In the few-shot classification setting where seen images are not sufficient, simply adopting the "pre-training&fine-tuning" paradigm does not produce better results.
The common practice to exploit CLIP pre-training knowledge and improve downstream generalization in few-shot classification is to fix CLIP pre-training weights while learning a lightweight module.
Tip-Adapter achieves large performance compared to both prompt-based methods and CLIP-Adapter on several classification datasets by fine-tuning a trainable query-key cache layer.

MF-Unit is obtained by an inductive representation of local feature maps on different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information to represent category-consistent characteristics.

Before model training, support set images are encoded into different-level features by the fixed CLIP visual encoder, then low-level feature maps are unfolded into Meta-Feature by a list of sliding windows with different scales.
MF-Unit is calculated by inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window, and is regarded as category-consistent features containing inductive knowledge.

During inference, the proposed MF-Adapter model first infers test images into MF-Units at different levels and different scales, then retrieves few-shot knowledge in the MF-Unit space of the support set to get local logits.
The final MF-Adapter prediction is combined with the original CLIP's high-level prediction, similar to Tip-Adapter.
The authors present comprehensive experiments on 11 widely-adopted datasets for few-shot classification and achieve state-of-the-art performance compared with previous CLIP-based methods.
CLIP and ALIGN are typical frameworks that leverage hundreds of millions of image-text pairs collected from the internet to align the embedding space of images with raw texts.
On top of CLIP, there are roughly two types of methods proposed to improve training strategy in recent few-shot learning tasks: prompt-based methods and adapter-based methods.

claim_records.text: The subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space.
The SRL framework measures similarity between two images according to a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.
Experimental results on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) demonstrate competitive/superior performance of the SRL method compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

claim_records.text: Metric-based few-shot image classification directly measures relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.
Existing local descriptor based works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.
The Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products as input and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples and assigns each query sample the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: DeepEMD employs the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute a structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance for few-shot image classification.
The EMD generates optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.
The cross-reference mechanism designed in DeepEMD can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
DeepEMD proposes a structured fully connected layer that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD to implement k-shot classification.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

DeepEMD outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on five widely used few-shot classification benchmarks: miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Fewshot-CIFAR100 (FC100), Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), and CIFAR-FewShot (CIFAR-FS).
DeepEMD demonstrates effectiveness on the image retrieval task in experiments.
The performance of non-optimization based methods often gets saturated quickly and increases slowly with more support samples available in k-shot 5-way tasks.
The structured fully connected layer of DeepEMD consistently outperforms baseline models, and shows even more advantages as the number of support images increases in k-shot 5-way tasks.
Comparison between DeepEMD and the finetuned cosine classifier shows advantages of structured prototypes and EMD as the metric in the proposed SFC layer.

claim_records.text: Cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification focuses on learning prior knowledge from a large number of labeled samples from source domains and then transferring the knowledge to tasks which contain few labeled samples in target domains.

Many current metric-based cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification methods first extract features of query and support samples, then directly predict the classes of query samples according to their distance to the support samples or prototypes.

The proposed multi-level relation learning method for cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification learns sample relations on different levels and incorporates them into the model learning process to improve classification performance.

Building on the method "Deep Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning for Hyperspectral Image Classification" which adopts a domain discriminator to deal with domain-level distribution difference, the proposed method applies contrastive learning to learn class-level sample relations to obtain more discriminable sample features.
The proposed method adopts a transformer based cross-attention learning module to learn set-level sample relations and acquire the attention from query samples to support samples.
Experimental results have demonstrated the contribution of the multi-level relation learning mechanism for few-shot hyperspectral image classification when compared with the state of the art methods.

claim_records.text: Few-shot classification aims to recognize unseen classes using very limited samples and is usually formulated as a metric learning problem.

The core issue of few-shot classification is how to learn consistent representations for images in both support and query sets, and effective metric learning for images between support and query sets.
The two core challenges of few-shot classification can be well modeled simultaneously via a unified Query-Support TransFormer (QSFormer) model.
The proposed QSFormer involves a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch.

sampleFormer aims to capture the dependence of samples in support and query sets for image representation, and adopts the Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model the Support, Query (image) representation and Metric learning for few-shot classification task.

A local patch Transformer is adopted as a complementary to the global learning branch to extract structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the proposed few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed multi-output embedding network maps samples into distinct feature spaces and extracts feature vectors at different stages, enabling the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.

Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.
Cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets achieved high accuracy in the testing domains for the proposed method.
The evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During the training phase, STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.
Extensive experiments show STN achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Meta-learning has been the most common framework for few-shot learning in recent years, and it learns the model from collections of few-shot classification tasks, which is believed to have a key advantage of making the training objective consistent with the testing objective.
Some recent works report that training for whole-classification (classification on the whole label-set) can get comparable or even better embedding than many meta-learning algorithms.
The edge between meta-learning and whole-classification lines of works for few-shot learning has yet been underexplored, and the effectiveness of meta-learning in few-shot learning remains unclear.

The explored simple process of meta-learning over a whole-classification pre-trained model on its evaluation metric achieves competitive performance to state-of-the-art methods on standard few-shot learning benchmarks.

fact_fields.method: meta-learning over a whole-classification pre-trained model on its evaluation metric

claim_records.text: Further analysis of the explored method sheds some light on understanding the trade-offs between the meta-learning objective and the whole-classification objective in few-shot learning.

fact_fields.method: analysis of meta-learning over whole-classification pre-trained model

claim_records.text: The practical transfer learning setting for few-shot learning involves training the network on common base classes with sufficient samples, then transferring the model to learn novel classes with a few examples.
The meta-learning framework for few-shot learning follows the key idea of learning to learn, and samples few-shot classification tasks from training samples.

Cosine classifier and Baseline++ perform whole-classification training by replacing the top linear layer with a cosine classifier, and adapt the classifier to few-shot classification tasks of novel classes via nearest centroid or fine-tuning a new layer respectively.
More advanced meta-learning methods set up new state-of-the-art results, and the effectiveness of whole-classification is revisited in two concurrent works with improved design choices.

The effectiveness of meta-learning compared to whole-classification in few-shot learning is still unclear, since the edge between whole-classification models and meta-learning models remains underexplored.

Experiments show a potential trade-off between the meta-learning and whole-classification objectives, which provides a clearer understanding of the comparison between both objectives for few-shot learning.

Classifier-Baseline trains the whole-classification model with a linear layer on the top and applies cosine nearest-centroid metric during test time for few-shot classification on novel classes, and does not replace the last layer with cosine classifier during training.
Meta-Baseline is meta-learning over a converged Classifier-Baseline on its evaluation metric (cosine nearest-centroid), and serves as a simple meta-learning baseline that has been overlooked.
The main purpose of Meta-Baseline in the paper is to understand the comparison between whole-classification and meta-learning objectives.

claim_records.text: Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) is proposed to fully affiliate the two disjoint sets of dense features in a bidirectional paradigm for few-shot classification.
In MCL, each local feature is associated with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL estimates class probability using features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process.
MCL is related to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged into existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that MCL achieves the state-of-the-art on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: A novel technique is proposed for synthesizing samples with multiple labels for the multi-label few-shot classification scenario.

The proposed method combines pairs of given examples in feature space, so that the resulting synthesized feature vectors correspond to examples whose label sets are obtained through certain set operations on the label sets of the corresponding input pairs.
The proposed method is capable of producing a sample containing the intersection, union or set-difference of labels present in two input samples.
The set operations used by the proposed method generalize to labels unseen during training.
The proposed method enables performing augmentation on examples of novel categories, facilitating multi-label few-shot classifier learning.

Numerous experiments show promising results for the label-set manipulation capabilities of the proposed approach, both directly using classification and retrieval metrics, and in the context of performing data augmentation for multi-label few-shot learning.
A benchmark is proposed for the multi-label few-shot learning task, and the proposed method compares favorably to all the common baselines on this benchmark.

claim_records.text: The proposed Deep Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DN4) is trained in an end-to-end manner built upon the episodic training mechanism for few-shot image classification.

DN4 replaces the image-level feature based measure in the final layer with a local descriptor based image-to-class measure, which is conducted online via k-nearest neighbor search over deep local descriptors of convolutional feature maps.

Experimental study on benchmark datasets shows DN4 achieves superiority over related state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods, with the largest absolute improvement of 17% over the next best method.

claim_records.text: The proposed Generative Dual Adversarial Network model for generalized zero-shot learning unifies three approaches: visual-to-semantic mapping, semantic-to-visual mapping, and metric learning.

The proposed model consists of a feature generator that generates visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to corresponding class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings, with all components trained under cyclic consistency loss combined with dual adversarial loss.

Experimental results show the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes, and performs better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: Existing cache-based adaptation approaches such as Tip-Adapter inherit CLIP's tendency to encode global, general-purpose representations that are not optimally discriminative for adapting the generalist model to the specialist's domain in low-data regimes.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

fact_fields.method: residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits

claim_records.text: Extensive evaluations on 11 benchmarks show consistent gains over state-of-the-art CLIP adapter and cache-based baselines while preserving zero-shot efficiency.

claim_records.text: The proposed Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) consists of a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to achieve the relational map from support and query samples.
Introducing Cosine Attention improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
The FS-CT method performs competitively on mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition was developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.

claim_records.text: 3D few-shot learning is more challenging than 2D FSL due to irregular structures, subtle inter-class differences, and high intra-class variances when trained on a low number of data.

The proposed Point-cloud Correlation Interaction (PCIA) network includes three plug-and-play components: Salient-Part Fusion (SPF) module, Self-Channel Interaction Plus (SCI+) module, and Cross-Instance Fusion Plus (CIF+) module.
The SPF, SCI+, and CIF+ modules can be inserted into most FSL algorithms with minor changes and significantly improve performance.
The PCIA method achieves state-of-the-art performance for the 3D FSL task on the ModelNet40-FS, ShapeNet70-FS, and ScanObjectNN-FS benchmark datasets.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, ensuring better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of CSRMs, the developed REP strengthens the extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.
Extensive experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks demonstrate that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios.
The code for HelixFormer is available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

# Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: An Embedding-to-Decision Comparison

## Abstract

This review compares few-shot metric learners by the part of the pipeline that carries the learning burden: transferable embeddings, support-set aggregation into class references, and fixed or learned similarity. Embedding losses such as K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet and ICNN seek compact, separated features; prototypes compress support examples into class means; distributional and subspace models represent uncertainty or variation; relation and region networks learn nonlinear or spatially explicit matches. Reported gains—including the roughly 2 percentage-point Proto-Triplet/ICNN gain on miniImageNet, SRL's competitive results on MiniImageNet/TieredImageNet/CUB, and RCN's effectiveness on four datasets—remain within the papers' chosen backbones, baselines and protocols. Cross-dataset tests support embedding transfer under domain shift, while Meta-Dataset/VTAB and SAR results show that rankings depend on data scale, adaptation protocol and modality. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3a7c251811c3] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:d7a3e9d6d024] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:c92e388de5e0:claim:c6694a2824d3] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:2400f60fdf99] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:1caf95a297b4] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:e63aa7133144] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:a7488a94c25a] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:da87ef976a14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:3331491a245d] [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:a2c594fa7649] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:4:b851ec357ca4:claim:56d300c5be2a] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:12:43376954155c:claim:b5e80a4f3431] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:61d34e2b3fa2] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2edc190258b3] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:fcaaac673d93] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:31b1ca19c83f] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:5d6069124699] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:09c9a02027f4] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:5e8d5050f5bd] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:b8986ea8c8ce] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:9:1354132472a1:claim:a5760c43bfed] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:45:924c867b4c98:claim:e1cf634f8522] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:d132e7c0300c]

The central scientific finding is therefore conditional complementarity rather than a universal winner. Fixed metrics and point prototypes are simple feed-forward choices when the embedding already satisfies the assumed geometry, learned comparators add relational flexibility, and richer class models can help when support observations reveal reliable variation. These benefits have boundaries: subspaces and distributions need sufficient independent support structure, learned relation modules can overfit episodic task distributions, and region explanations do not by themselves establish causal part importance or out-of-domain robustness. Direct numerical ranking is supported only inside matched tables or unified benchmarks. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:a7488a94c25a] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:da87ef976a14] [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:a2c594fa7649] [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:6d5b7a4a7ef3] [E:arxiv:2003.11539:section:abstract:2:44c3f540ed52:claim:f5ae08b23e3b] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:4:b851ec357ca4:claim:56d300c5be2a] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:12:43376954155c:claim:b5e80a4f3431] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:4:8a1d0545580d:claim:5b663af60cc2] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:61d34e2b3fa2] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:31b1ca19c83f] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:3331491a245d] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:e63aa7133144] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:5e8d5050f5bd] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:b8986ea8c8ce] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:d132e7c0300c]

## Introduction

Few-shot image classification asks a model to recognize query images from novel classes when only a small labeled support set is available. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised training can overfit when each novel class has very few examples; metric-learning methods address this by learning an embedding and/or comparison rule so that a query is classified from its similarity to support examples or class-level representations. This review therefore compares approaches by where they place the learning burden: transferable feature embeddings, aggregation of scarce support examples into class representations, and fixed or learned distance measures. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3a7c251811c3] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:3ec4f460da60] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:d94b7cd1d933] The common episodic formulation presents a support set with labeled images and a query set with unlabeled images from the same sampled task. A feature encoder maps images into a representation space, after which a metric function compares query features with support samples or class summaries. Early or canonical designs include nearest-sample comparison, class-mean prototypes, cosine or Euclidean distances, CNN-based relation modules, ridge regression, and graph-based comparison; these alternatives differ in whether similarity is predefined, learned, linear, nonlinear, local, or class-aggregated. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:d94b7cd1d933] [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:a2c594fa7649] [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:6d5b7a4a7ef3]

The organizing choice used here is the metric-learning pipeline rather than a universal taxonomy of all few-shot learning. Under that lens, embedding-focused methods seek features that generalize to unseen classes; class-representation methods convert one or several support images into points, distributions, or subspaces; and distance-learning methods train a comparator rather than relying only on a hand-specified geometric rule. This grouping is related to, but distinct from, optimization-based meta-learning that adapts parameters on a target task and large-scale transfer learning that pretrains upstream and later fine-tunes downstream. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3a7c251811c3] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:d7a3e9d6d024] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:c92e388de5e0:claim:c6694a2824d3]

Comparisons must also respect evaluation scope. Results within miniImageNet-style N-way, K-shot episodes do not automatically establish cross-domain robustness, and methods trained and tested under different episodic, transfer-learning, Meta-Dataset, VTAB, or domain-shift protocols are not directly rankable from isolated accuracy numbers. Later sections therefore separate mechanism, benchmark setting, dataset, backbone, shot count, metric, and reported result, and treat interpretability, subspace modeling, nonlinear comparison, embedding losses, and scale-based transfer as complementary dimensions rather than interchangeable claims of superiority. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:b8986ea8c8ce] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:9:1354132472a1:claim:a5760c43bfed] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:45:924c867b4c98:claim:e1cf634f8522] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:5d6069124699] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:61d34e2b3fa2]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

The taxonomy used in this review is organized around the metric-learning decision pipeline: what representation the encoder produces, how the scarce support examples are turned into a class-level reference, and how similarity or distance is then computed. This is a review-specific grouping for comparing few-shot metric learners, not a claim that the field has one universal taxonomy. It is also compatible with broader surveys that separate metric learning from optimization-based adaptation and transfer learning, while recognizing that these strategies can overlap: for example, an embedding used by a metric method may be trained with episodic meta-learning or transferred from large-scale pretraining. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3a7c251811c3] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:3ec4f460da60] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:d7a3e9d6d024] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:c92e388de5e0:claim:c6694a2824d3]

At the first stage, embedding-focused approaches treat the encoder as the main learned component. The target is a feature space in which samples from the same novel class lie close together and samples from different classes lie farther apart, even when the class labels were unseen during training. K-tuplet and related triplet-style losses explicitly use relationships among multiple samples, whereas later embedding-loss proposals such as Proto-Triplet and inter/intra-class nearest-neighbor losses directly shape intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. These methods remain metric-learning methods because the final decision still depends on feature comparison; their distinctive contribution is the geometry of the learned latent space rather than a separate target-task optimizer. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:2400f60fdf99] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:1caf95a297b4] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:e63aa7133144]

At the second stage, class-representation approaches differ in what occupies the reference side of the comparison. Sample-to-sample methods, including early Siamese and matching-style models, compare a query directly with individual support images. Point-prototype methods aggregate support embeddings, commonly by a simple or weighted mean, so that each class is represented by one reference vector. Distributional or subspace methods instead describe a class with more than a single point: a learned distribution with an associated divergence, or a low-dimensional subspace built from support features with query assignment based on projection or subspace distance. These representations encode progressively more assumptions about within-class variation, but they also require enough support structure to estimate the richer model. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:a7488a94c25a] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:da87ef976a14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:3331491a245d]

At the third stage, distance-measure approaches vary in how much of the comparison is learned. Fixed-rule methods use predefined geometry such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance to a class mean; they are simple and keep the comparator task-invariant, but their success depends heavily on the embedding satisfying that rule. Learned comparators use relation modules or other nonlinear functions to map paired query-support features into a match score. The relation-network rationale is that a transferable deep metric can express relationships that a fixed Euclidean or linear rule may not capture. Region Comparison Network carries this idea further by comparing local regions and exposing which query and support regions contribute to the match, adding an interpretability axis rather than merely changing the global score function. [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:a2c594fa7649] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:4:b851ec357ca4:claim:56d300c5be2a] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:12:43376954155c:claim:b5e80a4f3431] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:61d34e2b3fa2]

These stages should be read as comparison dimensions, not mutually exclusive classes. A subspace model still needs an encoder and a distance; a relation network still depends on an embedding; a K-tuplet network can be paired with a nonlinear distance module; and a region comparator combines local feature extraction with learned region-to-region matching. The useful distinction is where the method introduces its main inductive bias: generic discriminative embeddings, aggregation of support information, richer class geometry, nonlinear matching, or spatially explicit explanations. Consequently, two methods with the same broad label can make very different assumptions about feature locality, class variance, support-set size, and domain shift. [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:3331491a245d] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:61d34e2b3fa2] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:2400f60fdf99] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:1caf95a297b4]

Metric learning should also be distinguished from neighboring objectives that are sometimes conflated with it. Optimization-based meta-learning seeks parameters or update rules that can be adapted quickly to a task, whereas metric-based methods aim to avoid per-task inner-loop optimization by using a comparison rule at inference. Transfer learning pretrains on an upstream dataset and may fine-tune downstream; it can be a strong few-shot baseline, but pretraining alone does not make a model a metric learner. Zero-shot metric learning compares images with semantic class descriptions rather than labeled support images, and SAR few-shot classification changes both the image modality and benchmark distribution. Interpretability, cross-domain evaluation, runtime, and large-scale pretraining are therefore evaluation or design dimensions, not replacements for the embedding, class-representation, and distance-measure taxonomy.
