claim_records.text: Prototypical networks use squared Euclidean distance as the default Bregman divergence for computing distances to class prototypes.
Euclidean distance greatly outperforms cosine similarity as the distance function for prototypical networks.
Prototypical networks and matching networks become equivalent in the one-shot learning scenario.
Matching networks use sampled mini-batches called episodes during training, where each episode subsamples classes and data points to mimic the few-shot task.
Ravi and Larochelle propose a meta-learning approach to few-shot learning that trains an LSTM to produce updates to a classifier given an episode.

claim_records.text: The subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space.
The SRL framework measures similarity between two images according to a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.
Experimental results on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) demonstrate competitive/superior performance of the SRL method compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

claim_records.text: Metric-based few-shot image classification directly measures relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.
Existing local descriptor based works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.
The Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products as input and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples and assigns each query sample the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: DeepEMD employs the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute a structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance for few-shot image classification.
The EMD generates optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.
The cross-reference mechanism designed in DeepEMD can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
DeepEMD proposes a structured fully connected layer that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD to implement k-shot classification.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

DeepEMD outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on five widely used few-shot classification benchmarks: miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Fewshot-CIFAR100 (FC100), Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), and CIFAR-FewShot (CIFAR-FS).
DeepEMD demonstrates effectiveness on the image retrieval task in experiments.
The performance of non-optimization based methods often gets saturated quickly and increases slowly with more support samples available in k-shot 5-way tasks.
The structured fully connected layer of DeepEMD consistently outperforms baseline models, and shows even more advantages as the number of support images increases in k-shot 5-way tasks.
Comparison between DeepEMD and the finetuned cosine classifier shows advantages of structured prototypes and EMD as the metric in the proposed SFC layer.

fact_fields.method: structured fully connected layer vs finetuned cosine classifier

claim_records.text: Cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations may drive image-level embeddings from the same category far apart in a given metric space.
DeepEMD uses an optimal matching cost between image regions to represent image distance more faithfully for one-shot image classification.
DeepEMD formulates one-shot classification as an optimal matching problem that can be trained end-to-end, and uses a cross-reference mechanism to generate node weights for the EMD formulation.

Meta learning attempts to learn a model that can generalize to new tasks with minimum adaption effort.

claim_records.text: Cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification focuses on learning prior knowledge from a large number of labeled samples from source domains and then transferring the knowledge to tasks which contain few labeled samples in target domains.

Many current metric-based cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification methods first extract features of query and support samples, then directly predict the classes of query samples according to their distance to the support samples or prototypes.

The proposed multi-level relation learning method for cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification learns sample relations on different levels and incorporates them into the model learning process to improve classification performance.

Building on the method "Deep Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning for Hyperspectral Image Classification" which adopts a domain discriminator to deal with domain-level distribution difference, the proposed method applies contrastive learning to learn class-level sample relations to obtain more discriminable sample features.
The proposed method adopts a transformer based cross-attention learning module to learn set-level sample relations and acquire the attention from query samples to support samples.
Experimental results have demonstrated the contribution of the multi-level relation learning mechanism for few-shot hyperspectral image classification when compared with the state of the art methods.

Many current metric-based cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification methods first extract features of query and support samples, then directly predict the classes of query samples according to their distance to the support samples or prototypes.

The proposed multi-level relation learning method for cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral image classification learns sample relations on different levels and incorporates them into the model learning process to improve classification performance.

Building on the method "Deep Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning for Hyperspectral Image Classification" which adopts a domain discriminator to deal with domain-level distribution difference, the proposed method applies contrastive learning to learn class-level sample relations to obtain more discriminable sample features.
The proposed method adopts a transformer based cross-attention learning module to learn set-level sample relations and acquire the attention from query samples to support samples.
Experimental results have demonstrated the contribution of the multi-level relation learning mechanism for few-shot hyperspectral image classification when compared with the state of the art methods.

claim_records.text: Few-shot classification aims to recognize unseen classes using very limited samples and is usually formulated as a metric learning problem.

The core issue of few-shot classification is how to learn consistent representations for images in both support and query sets, and effective metric learning for images between support and query sets.
The two core challenges of few-shot classification can be well modeled simultaneously via a unified Query-Support TransFormer (QSFormer) model.
The proposed QSFormer involves a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch.

sampleFormer aims to capture the dependence of samples in support and query sets for image representation, and adopts the Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model the Support, Query (image) representation and Metric learning for few-shot classification task.

A local patch Transformer is adopted as a complementary to the global learning branch to extract structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the proposed few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed multi-output embedding network maps samples into distinct feature spaces and extracts feature vectors at different stages, enabling the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: A measure at only the image feature level may not be effective enough to generalize from base to novel classes when using only a few images.
The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification effectively captures local information by taking a multi-level descriptor of an image into consideration.
MLCN presents a self-correlation module and cross-correlation module to learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
MLCN proposes a pattern-correlation module to capture the pattern of fine-grained images and find relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used FSIC benchmarks.

ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on few-shot tasks from the mini-ImageNet dataset.
In few-shot experiments with domain shift, ProtoTransfer has comparable performance to supervised methods while requiring orders of magnitude fewer labels.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During the training phase, STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.
Extensive experiments show STN achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Meta-learning has been the most common framework for few-shot learning in recent years, and it learns the model from collections of few-shot classification tasks, which is believed to have a key advantage of making the training objective consistent with the testing objective.
Some recent works report that training for whole-classification (classification on the whole label-set) can get comparable or even better embedding than many meta-learning algorithms.
The edge between meta-learning and whole-classification lines of works for few-shot learning has yet been underexplored, and the effectiveness of meta-learning in few-shot learning remains unclear.

The explored simple process of meta-learning over a whole-classification pre-trained model on its evaluation metric achieves competitive performance to state-of-the-art methods on standard few-shot learning benchmarks.

fact_fields.method: meta-learning over a whole-classification pre-trained model on its evaluation metric

claim_records.text: Further analysis of the explored method sheds some light on understanding the trade-offs between the meta-learning objective and the whole-classification objective in few-shot learning.

fact_fields.method: analysis of meta-learning over whole-classification pre-trained model

claim_records.text: The practical transfer learning setting for few-shot learning involves training the network on common base classes with sufficient samples, then transferring the model to learn novel classes with a few examples.
The meta-learning framework for few-shot learning follows the key idea of learning to learn, and samples few-shot classification tasks from training samples.

Cosine classifier and Baseline++ perform whole-classification training by replacing the top linear layer with a cosine classifier, and adapt the classifier to few-shot classification tasks of novel classes via nearest centroid or fine-tuning a new layer respectively.
More advanced meta-learning methods set up new state-of-the-art results, and the effectiveness of whole-classification is revisited in two concurrent works with improved design choices.

The effectiveness of meta-learning compared to whole-classification in few-shot learning is still unclear, since the edge between whole-classification models and meta-learning models remains underexplored.

Experiments show a potential trade-off between the meta-learning and whole-classification objectives, which provides a clearer understanding of the comparison between both objectives for few-shot learning.

Classifier-Baseline trains the whole-classification model with a linear layer on the top and applies cosine nearest-centroid metric during test time for few-shot classification on novel classes, and does not replace the last layer with cosine classifier during training.
Meta-Baseline is meta-learning over a converged Classifier-Baseline on its evaluation metric (cosine nearest-centroid), and serves as a simple meta-learning baseline that has been overlooked.
The main purpose of Meta-Baseline in the paper is to understand the comparison between whole-classification and meta-learning objectives.

claim_records.text: The objective of the proposed method is to learn feature embeddings that generalize well under a linear classification rule for novel categories.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks represent each class by the mean embedding of the examples, and the classification rule is based on the distance to the nearest class mean.
Matching networks learns a kernel density estimate of the class densities using the embeddings over training data, and can also be interpreted as a form of attention over training examples.

The CIFAR-FS dataset is a recently proposed few-shot image classification benchmark consisting of all 100 classes from CIFAR-100, with classes randomly split into 64, 16 and 20 for meta-training, meta-validation, and meta-testing respectively, and each class contains 600 images of size 32 × 32.

The FC100 dataset is derived from CIFAR-100, containing 100 classes grouped into 20 superclasses, partitioned into 60 classes from 12 superclasses for meta-training, 20 classes from 4 superclasses for meta-validation, and 20 classes from 4 superclasses for meta-testing, with the goal of minimizing semantic overlap between classes.
Table 1 compares average few-shot classification accuracies (%) with 95% confidence intervals on miniImageNet and tieredImageNet meta-test splits for 5-way settings.
LEO makes use of encoder and relation network in addition to the WRN-28-10 backbone network to produce sample-dependent initialization.

The Matching Networks algorithm improves one-shot accuracy on Omniglot from 88.0% to 93.8% compared to competing approaches.

The usefulness of the same model is demonstrated on language modeling by introducing a one-shot task on the Penn Treebank.

The non-parametric approach to solving one-shot learning is based on two components: a model architecture following recent advances in neural networks augmented with memory, and a training strategy tailored for one-shot learning from the support set S.

An obvious drawback of the model is that as the support set S grows in size, the computation for each gradient update becomes more expensive.
One-shot experiments were run on three data sets: two image classification sets (Omniglot and ImageNet) and one language modeling set (Penn Treebank).

claim_records.text: Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) is proposed to fully affiliate the two disjoint sets of dense features in a bidirectional paradigm for few-shot classification.
In MCL, each local feature is associated with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL estimates class probability using features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process.
MCL is related to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged into existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that MCL achieves the state-of-the-art on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: A novel technique is proposed for synthesizing samples with multiple labels for the multi-label few-shot classification scenario.

The proposed method combines pairs of given examples in feature space, so that the resulting synthesized feature vectors correspond to examples whose label sets are obtained through certain set operations on the label sets of the corresponding input pairs.
The proposed method is capable of producing a sample containing the intersection, union or set-difference of labels present in two input samples.
The set operations used by the proposed method generalize to labels unseen during training.
The proposed method enables performing augmentation on examples of novel categories, facilitating multi-label few-shot classifier learning.

Numerous experiments show promising results for the label-set manipulation capabilities of the proposed approach, both directly using classification and retrieval metrics, and in the context of performing data augmentation for multi-label few-shot learning.
A benchmark is proposed for the multi-label few-shot learning task, and the proposed method compares favorably to all the common baselines on this benchmark.

claim_records.text: FoPro is a Few-shot guided Prototypical representation learning method that only requires a few labeled real-world examples to significantly improve performance in the real-world domain.
FoPro initializes each class center with few-shot real-world data as the 'realistic' prototype.
FoPro narrows the intra-class distance between web instances and 'realistic' prototypes via contrastive learning.
FoPro measures image-prototype distance with a learnable metric, and prototypes are polished by adjacent high-quality web images and involved in removing distant out-of-distribution samples.

fact_fields.method: Learnable metric for image-prototype distance measurement

claim_records.text: FoPro achieves state-of-the-art performance on three fine-grained datasets and two large-scale datasets when trained on web datasets with few real-world examples guided and evaluated on real-world datasets.
Compared with existing WSL methods under the same few-shot settings, FoPro excels in real-world generalization.

claim_records.text: The proposed Deep Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DN4) is trained in an end-to-end manner built upon the episodic training mechanism for few-shot image classification.

DN4 replaces the image-level feature based measure in the final layer with a local descriptor based image-to-class measure, which is conducted online via k-nearest neighbor search over deep local descriptors of convolutional feature maps.

Experimental study on benchmark datasets shows DN4 achieves superiority over related state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods, with the largest absolute improvement of 17% over the next best method.

claim_records.text: The proposed Generative Dual Adversarial Network model for generalized zero-shot learning unifies three approaches: visual-to-semantic mapping, semantic-to-visual mapping, and metric learning.

The proposed model consists of a feature generator that generates visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to corresponding class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings, with all components trained under cyclic consistency loss combined with dual adversarial loss.

Experimental results show the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes, and performs better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: Existing cache-based adaptation approaches such as Tip-Adapter inherit CLIP's tendency to encode global, general-purpose representations that are not optimally discriminative for adapting the generalist model to the specialist's domain in low-data regimes.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

fact_fields.method: residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits

claim_records.text: The proposed Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) consists of a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to achieve the relational map from support and query samples.
Introducing Cosine Attention improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
The FS-CT method performs competitively on mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition was developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.

The DeML framework's object-attention module is based on random walk graph propagation.
The DeML framework's channel-attention module is based on the adversary constraint.

claim_records.text: 3D few-shot learning is more challenging than 2D FSL due to irregular structures, subtle inter-class differences, and high intra-class variances when trained on a low number of data.

The proposed Point-cloud Correlation Interaction (PCIA) network includes three plug-and-play components: Salient-Part Fusion (SPF) module, Self-Channel Interaction Plus (SCI+) module, and Cross-Instance Fusion Plus (CIF+) module.
The SPF, SCI+, and CIF+ modules can be inserted into most FSL algorithms with minor changes and significantly improve performance.
The PCIA method achieves state-of-the-art performance for the 3D FSL task on the ModelNet40-FS, ShapeNet70-FS, and ScanObjectNN-FS benchmark datasets.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, ensuring better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of CSRMs, the developed REP strengthens the extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.
Extensive experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks demonstrate that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios.
The code for HelixFormer is available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning under low-data regimes, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration while ignoring that some descriptors are useless in classification due to their limited receptive field.

The paper argues that a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation should be established to explicitly select the query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters in FSL.
The proposed method is Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4) for few-shot learning.

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms existing state-of-the-arts on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.

The COSOC framework extracts foreground objects in images at both training and evaluation without any extra supervision to address background shortcut learning in FSL.
Extensive experiments on inductive FSL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the COSOC approach.

assertions.source_quote: This review compares few-shot metric learners by the part of the pipeline that carries the learning burden: transferable embeddings, support-set aggregation into class references, and fixed or learned similarity. Embedding losses such as K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet and ICNN seek compact, separated features; prototypes compress support examples into class means; distributional and subspace models represent uncertainty or variation; relation and region networks learn nonlinear or spatially explicit matches. Reported gains—including the roughly 2 percentage-point Proto-Triplet/ICNN gain on miniImageNet, SRL's competitive results on MiniImageNet/TieredImageNet/CUB, and RCN's effectiveness on four datasets—remain within the papers' chosen backbones, baselines and protocols. Cross-dataset tests support embedding transfer under domain shift, while Meta-Dataset/VTAB and SAR results show that rankings depend on data scale, adaptation protocol and modality. assertions.source_quote: Few-shot image classification asks a model to recognize query images from novel classes when only a small labeled support set is available. assertions.source_quote: The organizing choice used here is the metric-learning pipeline rather than a universal taxonomy of all few-shot learning. assertions.source_quote: At the first stage, embedding-focused approaches treat the encoder as the main learned component. The target is a feature space in which samples from the same novel class lie close together and samples from different classes lie farther apart, even when the class labels were unseen during training. K-tuplet and related triplet-style losses explicitly use relationships among multiple samples, whereas later embedding-loss proposals such as Proto-Triplet and inter/intra-class nearest-neighbor losses directly shape intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. These methods remain metric-learning methods because the final decision still depends on feature comparison; their distinctive contribution is the geometry of the learned latent space rather than a separate target-task optimizer. assertions.source_quote: At the first stage, embedding-focused approaches treat the encoder as the main learned component. The target is a feature space in which samples from the same novel class lie close together and samples from different classes lie farther apart, even when the class labels were unseen during training. K-tuplet and related triplet-style losses explicitly use relationships among multiple samples, whereas later embedding-loss proposals such as Proto-Triplet and inter/intra-class nearest-neighbor losses directly shape intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. assertions.source_quote: At the second stage, class-representation approaches differ in what occupies the reference side of the comparison. Sample-to-sample methods, including early Siamese and matching-style models, compare a query directly with individual support images. Point-prototype methods aggregate support embeddings, commonly by a simple or weighted mean, so that each class is represented by one reference vector. Distributional or subspace methods instead describe a class with more than a single point: a learned distribution with an associated divergence, or a low-dimensional subspace built from support features with query assignment based on projection or subspace distance. These representations encode progressively more assumptions about within-class variation, but they also require enough support structure to estimate the richer model. assertions.source_quote: At the third stage, distance-measure approaches vary in how much of the comparison is learned. Fixed-rule methods use predefined geometry such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance to a class mean; they are simple and keep the comparator task-invariant, but their success depends heavily on the embedding satisfying that rule. Learned comparators use relation modules or other nonlinear functions to map paired query-support features into a match score. The relation-network rationale is that a transferable deep metric can express relationships that a fixed Euclidean or linear rule may not capture. Region Comparison Network carries this idea further by comparing local regions and exposing which query and support regions contribute to the match, adding an interpretability axis rather than merely changing the global score function. assertions.source_quote: Metric learning should also be distinguished from neighboring objectives that are sometimes conflated with it. Optimization-based meta-learning seeks parameters or update rules that can be adapted quickly to a task, whereas metric-based methods aim to avoid per-task inner-loop optimization by using a comparison rule at inference. Transfer learning pretrains on an upstream dataset and may fine-tune downstream; it can be a strong few-shot baseline, but pretraining alone does not make a model a metric learner. Zero-shot metric learning compares images with semantic class descriptions rather than labeled support images, and SAR few-shot classification changes both the image modality and benchmark distribution. Interpretability, cross-domain evaluation, runtime, and large-scale pretraining are therefore evaluation or design dimensions, not replacements for the embedding, class-representation, and distance-measure taxonomy. assertions.source_quote: The applicability boundary of K-tuplet learning is that stronger embedding geometry does not remove the support-aggregation problem. The paper's contribution is therefore best read as evidence for the importance of feature embedding in metric-based few-shot learning, not as evidence that the comparator or class model is unnecessary. Its cross-domain experiments are also important because they train on miniImageNet and evaluate on other datasets; that setting tests domain shift more directly than reporting only novel classes sampled from the same benchmark. assertions.source_quote: Sample-to-sample comparison is the most direct class-reference design: a query is matched against individual labeled support images rather than a class summary. Early Siamese and matching-style methods fall in this group, and the review of deep metric learning notes their limited capacity to represent a novel class when support samples are scarce. Their mechanism is simple and avoids estimating a class mean or subspace from very few images, but a single support example can dominate the decision and within-class variation is represented only implicitly by the set of exemplars. This makes them a useful baseline family, but not necessarily a robust model of a class when K>1 information could be aggregated. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:9f8ad7e32aaa]

assertions.source_quote: Point-prototype methods replace individual exemplar matching with one reference vector per class. Prototypes may be a simple average of support embeddings, a weighted average, or a vector learned end-to-end. The contribution is data compression: several noisy support examples are pooled into a class-level representation that can be compared with a query using a fixed rule such as Euclidean distance or cosine similarity. This design is effective when support examples cluster around a meaningful class center, but it can collapse useful multimodal variation into one point. The review's discussion identifies point-based metric learning as sensitive to noise, which motivates distributional and subspace alternatives. The contribution is data compression: several noisy support examples are pooled into a class-level representation that can be compared with a query using a fixed rule such as Euclidean distance or cosine similarity. This design is effective when support examples cluster around a meaningful class center, but it can collapse useful multimodal variation into one point. The review's discussion identifies point-based metric learning as sensitive to noise, which motivates distributional and subspace alternatives. assertions.source_quote: Distributional class models move from a point estimate to uncertainty about class location. The reviewed variational Bayesian framework estimates a class distribution with a neural network and uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to compare a query with class models; it can also provide a confidence value for assigning the query to each class. This is a stronger statistical assumption than a prototype because the model must estimate distributional information from few support samples. Its potential benefit is calibrated or uncertainty-aware assignment, whereas its boundary is estimation reliability: with only one or highly correlated examples, an inferred distribution may be poorly constrained. The source supports this as a class-representation alternative, but does not make it directly comparable to subspace or relation-network results under a common benchmark table. assertions.source_quote: Subspace Representation Learning models each image as a subspace in a local CNN feature space rather than as one global vector, and compares images with a weighted subspace distance. The central mechanism is designed to preserve spatial structure and diversity within an image, properties that a global pooled vector can compress away. For K-shot tasks, SRL introduces two ways to aggregate support information: a prototypical subspace and a discriminative subspace. These template subspaces extend vector-based metric learning to subspace-based comparison. The method is evaluated on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB, with the authors reporting competitive or superior performance relative to prior state-of-the-art methods in their study. That claim is bounded by the paper's chosen baselines and protocol; it does not justify ranking SRL against methods evaluated only on other benchmarks or with substantially different training scale. [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:3331491a245d] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:fcaaac673d93]

assertions.source_quote: Deep Subspace Network is a related subspace approach in which each class is represented by a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples through singular value decomposition. A query is assigned by a nearest-subspace rule, specifically by the Euclidean distance from the query to its projection onto each class-specific subspace. The review reports that this construction is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network, reflecting the fact that a subspace can accommodate directions of class variation rather than forcing all support examples toward one mean. This advantage is conditional: constructing a useful class subspace requires multiple support features and meaningful variation, and very low-shot regimes may not provide enough observations to estimate it reliably. assertions.source_quote: SRL and DSN should therefore be understood as richer class-geometry models, not as free gains over prototypes. They address a specific weakness of point representations—loss of spatial or within-class diversity—by replacing a center with a subspace and a projection or weighted-distance decision. They are most applicable when local CNN features and multiple support observations reveal structure that survives subspace estimation. They are less directly motivated when the encoder already yields tightly clustered global vectors, when the support set is too small or redundant to estimate variation, or when interpretability rather than geometric robustness is the main objective. assertions.source_quote: Relation networks instead learn a nonlinear comparator. Rather than assuming that Euclidean distance or another fixed metric is the correct relation between query and support features, the method uses an embedding module plus a relation module that receives the paired representations and outputs a similarity score. The original rationale is that multiple learned nonlinear stages in both embedding and relation modules express a transferable deep metric, avoiding a manually fixed metric or a linear classifier. It is trained episodically end-to-end and can also be extended toward zero-shot recognition by replacing the support-image branch with a category-description branch. That zero-shot extension is a separate task setting; it should not be treated as evidence for few-shot accuracy when no labeled support images are present. assertions.source_quote: Region Comparison Network makes the comparison spatially explicit and interpretable. Instead of reducing each image to a global vector before matching, RCN compares local regions from query and support images inside the network and identifies related regions that contribute to the decision. Its Region Activation Mapping strategy visualizes intermediate variables to show which regions were used. The paper also describes generalizing explanations from the task level to the category level, which can be viewed as discovering prototypical parts that support the final prediction. Thus RCN combines a learned region-to-region metric with an explanation mechanism; its contribution is not merely another global similarity head. assertions.source_quote: Multi-stage embedding networks are a complementary way to enrich the representation side of metric learning. MSENet uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into different feature spaces, extracting vectors at multiple stages so that shallow, global, and abstract features can all contribute. Self-attention refines features at each stage, and learnable weights combine the stages. The authors motivate this design by arguing that traditional metric-based methods rely on a single distance between query and support features and therefore overlook shallow features. Its reported evaluation covers MiniImageNet and FC100 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot episodes, plus cross-domain tasks across eight datasets. This supports the method as a multi-level representation approach, but the available source quote does not supply a matched numerical table for direct comparison with RCN or SRL. [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:5e8d5050f5bd]

assertions.source_quote: Hybrid and neighboring approaches clarify where pure metric methods end. Meta-Metric-Learner combines a task-specific metric-based base learner with a meta-learner that learns to specify the base model. Its stated motivation is that a single task-invariant metric assumes tasks come from similar domains, while optimization-style handling can support flexible task structure; the hybrid is intended to allow varying numbers of classes and produce more generalized metrics across tasks. This differs from a conventional metric learner that fixes one comparator across all tasks. assertions.source_quote: Large-scale transfer learning is not itself a metric-learning mechanism, but it is a crucial comparator for metric methods. BiT-style transfer pretrains a large network upstream and fine-tunes downstream; the cross-family study finds that, on average, large-scale transfer methods outperform competing approaches on Meta-Dataset even when trained only on ImageNet, while meta-learning methods struggle on VTAB when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset. The same study cautions that scale does not solve highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. These findings challenge isolated claims from episodic metric learners: a simple, well-engineered pretrained representation may be competitive, but transfer and metric-learning numbers are only rankable when training data, model capacity, fine-tuning, and benchmark protocol are aligned. assertions.source_quote: Experimental comparison should start from protocol rather than from a single leaderboard number. The standard episodic setting samples N-way, K-shot support and query tasks, usually with 1–5 labeled examples per class, and metric methods are judged by classification accuracy averaged over many sampled tasks. However, the available evidence spans several non-equivalent regimes: same-benchmark novel-class episodes on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CUB, FC100 and related datasets; cross-domain tests in which a model trained on MiniImageNet is evaluated on CUB, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars, Caltech-101 or other datasets; Meta-Dataset and VTAB-style cross-family evaluation; and specialized SAR target classification. These settings ask different questions, so an accuracy on one dataset cannot be ranked against an accuracy on another without matching backbone, training data, episodic sampler, shot count, preprocessing, transductiveness, fine-tuning and evaluation episodes. assertions.source_quote: Within conventional same-domain episodic benchmarks, the strongest supported comparison is qualitative rather than a universal ranking. Embedding-focused K-tuplet learning reports that it outperforms other metric-based methods on miniImageNet and is competitive with meta-based methods, but the source quote does not provide a matched table of exact accuracies, confidence intervals or all backbone settings. Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses report a gain of about 2 percentage points over compared metric-based methods on miniImageNet and competitive cross-domain behavior on CUB, Dogs and Cars. SRL reports competitive or superior performance relative to prior state-of-the-art methods included in its study on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and CUB. RCN reports effectiveness over existing baselines on four benchmark datasets. These are all favorable within-paper findings, but because the cited records do not expose identical backbones and baselines, they should not be collapsed into a claim that one metric-learning family is globally best. assertions.source_quote: The clearest dimension on which the methods differ is the component changed in the metric pipeline. K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN primarily alter representation learning: K-tuplet compares an anchor jointly with K negatives and uses semi-hard mining, whereas Proto-Triplet/ICNN explicitly encode intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. Prototypical or nearest-mean methods alter class aggregation by representing each class with a mean vector and applying a fixed geometric decision. Relation networks alter the decision rule by learning a nonlinear comparator from paired query and support features. RCN also learns a comparator, but its experimental contribution includes local region correspondence and Region Activation Mapping interpretability, not only accuracy. SRL and DSN alter class geometry by replacing or supplementing point vectors with subspaces; SRL uses weighted subspace distance plus prototypical or discriminative template subspaces, while DSN uses SVD-constructed class subspaces and projection distance. Prototypical or nearest-mean methods alter class aggregation by representing each class with a mean vector and applying a fixed geometric decision. Relation networks alter the decision rule by learning a nonlinear comparator from paired query and support features. RCN also learns a comparator, but its experimental contribution includes local region correspondence and Region Activation Mapping interpretability, not only accuracy. SRL and DSN alter class geometry by replacing or supplementing point vectors with subspaces; SRL uses weighted subspace distance plus prototypical or discriminative template subspaces, while DSN uses SVD-constructed class subspaces and projection distance. assertions.source_quote: Cross-domain experiments separate embedding robustness from in-domain episodic fit more directly. Deep K-tuplet Network was trained on miniImageNet and then evaluated on novel classes in Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars; the authors report that it significantly outperforms prior methods in that cross-dataset setting and interpret the result as evidence that the learned discriminative embedding generalizes beyond the training dataset. The Proto-Triplet/ICNN study similarly reports competitive generalization to CUB, Dogs and Cars. MSENet reports cross-domain testing across eight benchmark datasets after evaluating 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot tasks on MiniImageNet and FC100. These results support the embedding-side hypothesis that transferable feature geometry helps under domain shift, but the studies do not provide enough matched information in the cited excerpts to compare their exact cross-domain accuracies with each other or to attribute gains solely to the loss when architecture and training details differ. assertions.source_quote: Subspace methods are supported by a different experimental argument: richer class descriptions can reduce sensitivity to noisy or outlying support examples. The deep metric-learning review states that Deep Subspace Network, which builds low-dimensional class subspaces from support samples and assigns a query by distance to its projection, is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network. SRL evaluates its image-level subspace representation and K-shot prototypical or discriminative template subspaces on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and CUB and reports competitive or superior performance compared with previous state-of-the-art methods in its experiments. These findings are directly relevant when local spatial structure and within-image or within-class diversity are lost by global vector pooling, but they do not establish superiority in one-shot settings where estimating a subspace from support variation may be poorly constrained. assertions.source_quote: RCN's experiments should be interpreted along both accuracy and explainability axes. The method compares related local regions between query and support images and uses Region Activation Mapping to visualize intermediate comparison variables. Its paper reports extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets and effectiveness over existing baselines, while also generalizing explanations from tasks to categories and identifying prototypical parts. This makes RCN comparatively strong on the sourced criterion of interpretable local matching. It is not experimentally interchangeable with SRL: RCN exposes region-to-region evidence for a match, whereas SRL preserves spatial structure through subspace representations and weighted subspace distance. Without a common table using the same encoder, episodes and baselines, the cited evidence supports complementarity rather than a numerical ranking between region explanations and subspace geometry. assertions.source_quote: Fixed-metric and learned-metric methods also trade simplicity for flexibility. Cosine matching, Euclidean distance to class means, ridge regression and graph-based comparison are surveyed as metric-learning choices, while relation networks explicitly learn a nonlinear relation module instead of relying on a fixed metric. The empirical implication is that fixed rules are easier to deploy and remain feed-forward, but they can only separate classes well when the encoder and class representation already satisfy the metric geometry. Learned relation modules can model more complex match relations, but their reported gains depend on episodic training and may reflect comparator overfitting if the training task distribution differs from the test domain. The cited sources support this mechanism-level trade-off; they do not supply a universal accuracy advantage for learned over fixed distances across all benchmarks. assertions.source_quote: The cross-family Meta-Dataset/VTAB study is an important warning against treating episodic metric results as isolated evidence of best few-shot performance. It compares leading transfer and meta-learning approaches under both Meta-Dataset and VTAB and finds that, on average, large-scale BiT transfer methods outperform competing approaches on Meta-Dataset even when trained only on ImageNet, whereas meta-learning approaches trained and validated on Meta-Dataset struggle to compete on VTAB. The same study reports that increasing scale does not improve performance on highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. Because BiT is a large-scale pretraining and fine-tuning comparator rather than a pure metric learner, this result does not show that transfer is a better metric; it shows that metric methods must be compared under matched data scale and adaptation protocol before claiming state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy. assertions.source_quote: The cross-family Meta-Dataset/VTAB study is an important warning against treating episodic metric results as isolated evidence of best few-shot performance. It compares leading transfer and meta-learning approaches under both Meta-Dataset and VTAB and finds that, on average, large-scale BiT transfer methods outperform competing approaches on Meta-Dataset even when trained only on ImageNet, whereas meta-learning approaches trained and validated on Meta-Dataset struggle to compete on VTAB. The same study reports that increasing scale does not improve performance on highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. Because BiT is a large-scale pretraining and fine-tuning comparator rather than a pure metric learner, this result does not show that transfer is a better metric; it shows that metric methods must be compared under matched data scale and adaptation protocol before claiming state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy. assertions.source_quote: Specialized modalities further limit generalization of natural-image rankings. The FewSAR benchmark for few-shot SAR target classification implements 15 classic methods in three categories, establishes common protocols, and analyzes both quantitative results and runtime under the same setting. Its authors observe that metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy in that SAR testbed, while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, which they attribute primarily to bias in existing datasets. This is evidence for metric learning within the SAR benchmark and protocol, not evidence that the same ranking holds for MiniImageNet, CUB or Meta-Dataset. It also illustrates why runtime and dataset bias, when measured under a unified benchmark, are useful comparison dimensions that most natural-image method quotes do not provide. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:d132e7c0300c]

assertions.source_quote: Taken together, the sourced experiments support conditional conclusions rather than a single winner. Embedding-loss methods are best supported for improving latent-space separation and cross-dataset transfer in their reported protocols; point prototypes and fixed metrics offer simple feed-forward baselines; relation and region networks add learned nonlinear or local matching, with RCN additionally providing visual explanations; distributional and subspace models target uncertainty, spatial structure and robustness to support noise; and multi-stage encoders target the use of shallow through abstract features. Direct numerical ranking is possible only inside a paper's matched table or a unified benchmark such as the SAR study or the controlled cross-family transfer/meta study. Across the other cited papers, unmatched datasets, backbones, training sources, shot counts, class-representation assumptions and fine-tuning regimes make isolated accuracy claims non-comparable, even when each paper individually reports competitive or superior performance. assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is that metric learning does not remove the fundamental few-shot estimation risk; it moves it among the encoder, class representation, and comparator. With only a few labeled examples, a point prototype can be distorted by noise, a distribution can be under-identified, and a subspace can be poorly estimated unless support observations contain enough independent variation. The review's note that point-based representations are sensitive to noise explains why distributional and subspace models are attractive, but it also defines their boundary: richer class models need more than a nominal K-shot count if the available images are redundant, correlated, or atypical. Thus, robustness gains over a class mean should be interpreted as conditional on support quality and shot count, not as automatic benefits in every 1-shot task. assertions.source_quote: A second problem is the tension between fixed and learned distance measures. Fixed Euclidean, cosine, or prototype-distance rules are simple and feed-forward, but they classify correctly only when the encoder has already arranged novel-class queries to satisfy the assumed geometry. Learned relation modules relax that assumption by training a nonlinear comparator, yet their flexibility must be learned from episodic tasks and can overfit the training task distribution; the original relation-network argument for a transferable deep metric therefore does not imply that a learned comparator is universally preferable. Comparisons need matched backbones, episodes, and novel-task domains before the extra comparator capacity can be credited for an accuracy difference. assertions.source_quote: Domain shift is a separate and especially concrete limitation. Standard episodes in which base and novel classes are sampled from the same dataset can favor a task-invariant metric, while real deployment may move from miniImageNet-like training data to birds, dogs, cars, or other visual domains. The K-tuplet work explicitly motivates cross-dataset evaluation because same-dataset novel-class testing may not represent real-world generalization, and the metric-learning literature also reports that existing metric approaches often fail to generalize well across domains. This means strong same-domain episodic accuracy is not sufficient evidence that an embedding, prototype rule, or relation module will transfer across datasets. assertions.source_quote: Domain shift is a separate and especially concrete limitation. Standard episodes in which base and novel classes are sampled from the same dataset can favor a task-invariant metric, while real deployment may move from miniImageNet-like training data to birds, dogs, cars, or other visual domains. The K-tuplet work explicitly motivates cross-dataset evaluation because same-dataset novel-class testing may not represent real-world generalization, and the metric-learning literature also reports that existing metric approaches often fail to generalize well across domains. This means strong same-domain episodic accuracy is not sufficient evidence that an embedding, prototype rule, or relation module will transfer across datasets. assertions.source_quote: The assumption of one shared metric across tasks is itself restrictive. A metric trained to be invariant across all episodic tasks can support different numbers of classes, but it is most credible when tasks come from sufficiently similar domains; when task structure or domain varies, a single uniform comparator may not describe all query-support relationships. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper identifies this issue directly and motivates a task-specific metric learner specified by a meta-learner. That hybrid direction shows the trade-off clearly: pure metric methods avoid target-task parameter updates, but adapting or specifying the metric can improve flexibility at the cost of added meta-learning complexity. assertions.source_quote: Representation learning also faces unresolved geometric trade-offs. Triplet, K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and nearest-neighbor-style losses can encourage intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, but enforcing a simple geometry may be inappropriate when classes are multimodal or when background, pose, and viewpoint create legitimate within-class spread. K-tuplet learning addresses the narrow one-negative triplet update by comparing against multiple negatives and mining semi-hard examples, while later Proto-Triplet/ICNN losses directly target inter- and intra-class distances. These designs improve the embedding under their reported protocols, but they do not solve class aggregation, local correspondence, uncertainty, or domain shift by themselves. assertions.source_quote: Spatial information creates another trade-off. Global vector representations are compact and easy to compare, but SRL argues that they can discard spatial structure and within-image diversity; its subspace representation and weighted subspace distance are designed to retain that information. RCN approaches a related problem from the interpretability side by comparing local regions and visualizing the regions that support a decision. These are complementary responses, not interchangeable solutions: preserving local structure in a subspace does not necessarily provide human-readable region correspondence, and region explanations do not necessarily estimate class-level variation or outlier robustness. assertions.source_quote: Interpretability remains incomplete even when a network exposes salient regions. RCN's Region Activation Mapping and task-to-category generalization can reveal related query-support regions and prototypical parts, which addresses a gap in metric methods that mainly output a scalar similarity score. assertions.source_quote: Evaluation norms are a major source of unresolved disagreement. The cross-family Meta-Dataset/VTAB study argues that transfer and meta-learning advances have often been measured in isolation, making direct comparison difficult because of divergent evaluation norms. Large-scale BiT transfer is reported to be a remarkably competitive and robust baseline on average, including on Meta-Dataset when trained only on ImageNet, but scale does not improve highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks and meta-learners trained on Meta-Dataset struggle on VTAB. Consequently, an episodic metric method's state-of-the-art claim is narrow unless training data scale, model capacity, fine-tuning, validation source, and downstream benchmark are matched. assertions.source_quote: Benchmark and modality dependence further limits general conclusions. The FewSAR study finds that metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy in its unified SAR target-classification testbed, while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, and attributes that pattern partly to existing dataset bias. This is useful controlled evidence for SAR, but it cannot be generalized into a ranking for natural-image benchmarks. Conversely, natural-image results from MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CUB, or FC100 should not be assumed to hold for SAR. Runtime and dataset bias are meaningful only when measured under a common protocol, which most isolated method papers do not provide. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:d132e7c0300c]

unsupported_claims.source_quote: Deep Subspace Network is a related subspace approach in which each class is represented by a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples through singular value decomposition. A query is assigned by a nearest-subspace rule, specifically by the Euclidean distance from the query to its projection onto each class-specific subspace. The review reports that this construction is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network, reflecting the fact that a subspace can accommodate directions of class variation rather than forcing all support examples toward one mean. This advantage is conditional: constructing a useful class subspace requires multiple support features and meaningful variation, and very low-shot regimes may not provide enough observations to estimate it reliably. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Relation networks instead learn a nonlinear comparator. Rather than assuming that Euclidean distance or another fixed metric is the correct relation between query and support features, the method uses an embedding module plus a relation module that receives the paired representations and outputs a similarity score. The original rationale is that multiple learned nonlinear stages in both embedding and relation modules express a transferable deep metric, avoiding a manually fixed metric or a linear classifier. It is trained episodically end-to-end and can also be extended toward zero-shot recognition by replacing the support-image branch with a category-description branch. That zero-shot extension is a separate task setting; it should not be treated as evidence for few-shot accuracy when no labeled support images are present. It also remains a feed-forward metric approach in the cited formulation: no target-task fine-tuning is required. The method's contribution is therefore the learned comparison function, while its evidence must be assessed against fixed-metric methods using matched backbones and episodes. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The assumption of one shared metric across tasks is itself restrictive. A metric trained to be invariant across all episodic tasks can support different numbers of classes, but it is most credible when tasks come from sufficiently similar domains; when task structure or domain varies, a single uniform comparator may not describe all query-support relationships. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper identifies this issue directly and motivates a task-specific metric learner specified by a meta-learner. That hybrid direction shows the trade-off clearly: pure metric methods avoid target-task parameter updates, but adapting or specifying the metric can improve flexibility at the cost of added meta-learning complexity. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Representation learning also faces unresolved geometric trade-offs. Triplet, K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and nearest-neighbor-style losses can encourage intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, but enforcing a simple geometry may be inappropriate when classes are multimodal or when background, pose, and viewpoint create legitimate within-class spread. K-tuplet learning addresses the narrow one-negative triplet update by comparing against multiple negatives and mining semi-hard examples, while later Proto-Triplet/ICNN losses directly target inter- and intra-class distances. These designs improve the embedding under their reported protocols, but they do not solve class aggregation, local correspondence, uncertainty, or domain shift by themselves.
